blocks.text:
Every Java program is full of strings: names, log lines, JSON, SQL, keys of maps. Because they are everywhere, the design of `java.lang.String` shapes the speed and memory of whole applications. Interviewers love this class for the same reason: a handful of simple facts (immutability, the pool, `==` versus `equals`) explain a surprising number of bugs. In this chapter you will learn what a `String` really is in memory, why it is immutable, how the string pool works, what `+` compiles to, when to use `StringBuilder`, and the methods you should know by heart.

### What a String is

A `String` is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units. Immutable means that once the object exists, no method can change its content. Every method that looks like a modification (`toUpperCase`, `replace`, `concat`, `substring`) returns a new `String` and leaves the original alone.

blocks.title: Immut.java

blocks.code:
$ java Immut.java
hello HELLO
hello world
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The second line of `main` is the classic beginner bug: calling `concat` and ignoring the result does nothing. The variable `s` is a reference; the last line moves the reference to a new object. The old `"hello"` object is untouched (and becomes garbage if nothing else points to it).

#### Why immutable?

The designers chose immutability for reasons that still matter today:

- **Safety as a map key and in sets.** `hashCode` is computed from the content. If content could change, an entry would be lost inside a `HashMap` after mutation. `String` also caches its hash in a field, so repeated lookups are cheap.
- **Security.** Class names, file paths, and network host names are strings. A checked path cannot be changed by another thread between the check and the use.
- **Thread safety for free.** Any number of threads can share a `String` without locks.
- **Sharing.** The JVM can share one object between all places that use the same literal (the string pool, below).

### Inside the object: byte[] and coder

Until Java 8, a `String` held a `char[]`, two bytes per character. Most strings in real programs are Latin-1 (English letters, digits, punctuation), so half the memory was wasted. **Compact strings** (JEP 254, Java 9) changed the internals. A `String` now holds:

- `value`: a `byte[]` with the characters.
- `coder`: a byte, `0` = LATIN1 (one byte per char) or `1` = UTF16 (two bytes per char).
- `hash`: the cached hash code (and a flag saying whether it has been computed).

If every character of the string is in the range U+0000 to U+00FF, the JVM stores one byte per character; if even one character is outside that range, the whole string is stored as UTF-16. The feature is on by default (`-XX:+CompactStrings`); the API behaves identically, so you never see it except as lower memory use. You can confirm the flag on your machine:

blocks.code:
$ java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep CompactStrings
     bool CompactStrings         = true         {pd product} {default}
blocks.title: Check the flag

blocks.text: The cost of the feature is a tiny check on each operation to see which encoding applies; the benefit is that heaps full of ASCII text (logs, JSON, identifiers) shrink noticeably. `length()` still counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: You can find the private `coder` field with reflection, but `setAccessible(true)` on it fails on a modern JDK because of strong encapsulation (JEP 403, Java 17). That is deliberate. Use `getBytes(StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1).length` or a heap analyser if you must measure.

### The string pool and intern

Programs create the same literal many times: `"OK"`, `"id"`, `"GET"`. The JVM keeps a table of unique strings called the **string pool** (or string intern table). When the class loader resolves a string literal, the JVM looks it up in the pool: if an equal string is there, the existing object is used; if not, a new one is created and added. Since Java 7 the pool lives in the ordinary heap (before that it sat in PermGen), so pooled strings can be garbage-collected when nothing refers to them. The table is a hash table whose size is tunable with `-XX:StringTableSize` (the default here is 65536 buckets).

blocks.text: Four expressions create strings in different ways. Run this and predict each line before you look at the answer:

blocks.title: PoolDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java PoolDemo.java
a == b          : true
a == c          : false
a.equals(c)     : true
a == d (intern) : true
a == e (runtime): false
a == f (const)  : true
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `a == b`: both literals resolve to the same pooled object.
- `new String("java")` always allocates a fresh object, so `a == c` is false although the content is equal. `new` `String(String)` is almost never useful; it only creates garbage.
- `intern()` returns the pooled instance with that content (adding one if needed), so `d` is the same object as `a`.
- `"ja" + "va"` is a **constant expression**: the compiler folds it into the literal `"java"` at compile time. `part + "va"` involves a non-final variable, so it is computed at run time and produces a new object. (If `part` were declared `final` `String part = "ja";` it would be a constant variable and `e` would be pooled too.)

#### == versus equals

`==` on references asks "are these the same object?". `equals` asks "do these have the same content?". For strings you almost always want `equals`. Comparing with `==` seems to work in tests because literals are pooled, and then fails in production when the value comes from user input, a file, or a database. To avoid a `NullPointerException`, write the literal first: `"admin".equals(role)`, or use `java.util.Objects.equals(a, b)`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Never rely on `==` for strings, even "just this once". Whether two equal strings are the same object depends on how each was created. Static analysers flag it for a reason.

#### When is intern() worth it?

`intern()` can save memory when you load millions of strings drawn from a small set of values (country codes, status names) and keep them for a long time. It has costs: a lookup in the global table on every call, and the table is a shared resource. In most code a `HashMap<String,String>` of your own, or simply not worrying, is better. Modern JVMs also offer string deduplication in G1 (`-XX:+UseStringDeduplication`), which shares the `byte[]` of equal strings during garbage collection without changing identity.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How many objects does `String s = new String("abc");` create? At most two: the literal `"abc"` in the pool (created when the class is resolved, only if not already there) and one new `String` object on the heap. `s` refers to the heap object. If `"abc"` was already pooled, only one new object is created by this statement.

### Concatenation: + and what it compiles to

The `+` operator on strings is syntax sugar; the compiler decides what to emit. Before Java 9 `javac` generated a hidden `StringBuilder` and chained `append` calls. Since Java 9 (JEP 280) it emits a single `invokedynamic` instruction that calls `StringConcatFactory`. The JVM picks the best strategy at the first execution: it can compute the exact final length, allocate the right array once, and copy the parts, which beats a `StringBuilder` chain. You can see it in bytecode:

blocks.title: Indy.java

blocks.code:
$ javac Indy.java && javap -c -p Indy
  static java.lang.String f(java.lang.String, int);
    Code:
       0: aload_0
       1: iload_1
       2: invokedynamic #7,  0   // InvokeDynamic #0:makeConcatWithConstants:(...)
       7: areturn
blocks.title: Trimmed javap output

blocks.text:
The constant parts of the expression (`"id="` and `", n="`) are stored once as a recipe string in the constant pool, with placeholders for the two arguments. Target 8 (`javac --release 8`) still produces the `StringBuilder` form because indy concatenation needs a Java 9+ runtime.

### StringBuilder and StringBuffer

A single `+` is fine. The trouble is `+` (or `+=`) in a loop: each iteration creates a new `String` and copies everything built so far, so building a string of length n costs O(n squared) character copies. `StringBuilder` is a mutable buffer: `append` writes into spare capacity and only grows the array occasionally (the new capacity is roughly double plus 2).

blocks.code:
$ java Perf.java
n=10,000  +=: 63 ms   StringBuilder: 0 ms
n=50,000  +=: 1083 ms   StringBuilder: 2 ms
n=100,000  +=: 1783 ms   StringBuilder: 4 ms

Look at the shape, not the exact milliseconds: doubling the input makes `+=` roughly quadratic, while `StringBuilder` stays linear. This is a crude measurement (no JMH, one run); the conclusion is the well-known one.

You can watch the buffer grow. A default `StringBuilder` starts with capacity 16 and, on overflow, grows to roughly `old` `* 2 + 2`:

blocks.text: `StringBuffer` is the old thread-safe variant. Its per-call locking is almost never what you want: a buffer shared between threads rarely makes sense, and the lock does not make a sequence of calls atomic. Use `StringBuilder` unless you are maintaining old code. Useful `StringBuilder` methods: `append`, `insert`, `delete`, `deleteCharAt`, `reverse`, `setCharAt`, `setLength`, `indexOf`, `toString`.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: A loop that builds output with `+=` can often be replaced by `String.join(", ", list)`, `Collectors.joining`, or `String.repeat`. They use a builder internally and say what you mean.

### The methods you should know

The next listing exercises the methods that appear most often in code and interviews. Read each line, predict the result, then compare with the output.

blocks.title: Methods.java

blocks.code:
$ java Methods.java
13 11
true true
ababab
[a, b, c]
Asha scored 91.5
a|b|c
4
6
[a, b, c]
[] 1
[]
3 5
-4 -1
99162322 2112 2112
null xnull
Hello!
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Points worth learning from that output:

- `trim` **vs** `strip`**.** `trim()` (Java 1.0) removes only characters up to U+0020. `strip()` (Java 11) removes all Unicode whitespace as defined by `Character.isWhitespace`, including the em space, so it trimmed two more characters here. Prefer `strip`, `stripLeading`, `stripTrailing`. `isBlank()` is true for empty or whitespace-only strings.
- `lines()` splits on `\n`, `\r`, and `\r\n` and returns a `Stream<String>`.
- `split` **drops trailing empty strings.** `"a,b,,c,,".split(",")` gives 4 parts, not 6; pass a negative limit to keep them. The pattern is a regular expression, so `split(".")` matches every character and returns nothing; use `split("\\.")` for a literal dot. `"".split(",")` returns an array with one empty string, not an empty array. More on regex in the next chapter.
- `compareTo` returns the difference of the first differing chars (`'v'` - `'z'` = -4); rely only on its sign.
- **Equal hash codes do not imply equal strings.** `"Aa"` and `"BB"` collide. The formula is `s[0]*31^(n-1) + ... +` `s[n-1]`, which is exactly the `hashCode` that `HashMap` buckets use.
- `"x" + null` gives `"xnull"`: concatenation converts `null` to the text `null`.

Other everyday methods: `charAt`, `substring(begin, end)` (end exclusive; copies, not a view, since Java 7u6), `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `replace(CharSequence, CharSequence)` (literal), `replaceAll` (regex), `toLowerCase`, `valueOf`, `chars()`, `toCharArray`, `indent`, `stripIndent`, `translateEscapes`, and `String.valueOf` for turning anything into text.

### switch on strings

Since Java 7 a `switch` can select on a `String`. It uses `equals` semantics (internally a `hashCode` switch followed by an `equals` check), so it is case-sensitive and a `null` selector throws `NullPointerException`. With Java 14 switch expressions the code is short:

blocks.title: SwitchOnString.java

blocks.code:
$ java SwitchOnString.java
1 2 0
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: Case labels must be constant expressions, so you cannot use a variable as a label. Normalise the selector (`day.strip().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)`) when input comes from users; the chapter on Unicode and Locale explains why `Locale.ROOT` matters there.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring applications you meet strings mostly at boundaries: request parameters, JSON fields, SQL text, log messages. Two habits pay off. First, log with placeholders (`log.info("order {} failed", id)`) so no string is built when the level is disabled. Second, never build SQL by concatenating user input; use prepared statements. The concatenation itself is cheap, but the injection risk is not.

### Strings in everyday text processing

Most string work is a small number of recurring recipes. The program below counts word frequencies in a text block, builds a delimited string three ways, and shows the `split` edge cases that surprise people.

blocks.title: Wf.java

blocks.code:
$ java Wf.java
{be=2, in=1, is=1, mind=1, nobler=1, not=1, or=1, question=1,
 suffer=1, that=1, the=2, tis=1, to=3, whether=1}
[to=3, be=2, the=2]
EMPTY
{a, b} x|y|z
2
h-e-l-l-o
true
2112 2112 false
0
4 6 [, x, , y]
blocks.title: Output (the first line is one line in reality; wrapped here)

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `split("\\W+")` splits on runs of non-word characters. The regex is a `String`, so the backslash is doubled. A text block (`"""`) keeps the original line breaks, which `\W+` also treats as separators.
- `Collectors.groupingBy(..., TreeMap::new, counting())` gives a sorted frequency table in one pipeline; Part 7 explains collectors.
- `String.join`, `StringJoiner` and `Collectors.joining` all insert a delimiter *between* elements, so there is no trailing comma to trim. `StringJoiner` also supports a prefix, a suffix and a value for the empty case.
- `chars()` yields an `IntStream` of UTF-16 code units; cast to `char` to rebuild text. Use `codePoints()` when characters outside the BMP are possible (see the Unicode chapter).
- `"Aa"` and `"BB"` have the same `hashCode` (2112) but are not equal. Equal hash codes do not imply equal objects, which is exactly why `HashMap` still calls `equals`. `String` caches its hash code in a field after the first call, so using strings as map keys is cheap.
- `"a,b,,c,,".split(",")` returns 4 elements, because trailing empty strings are removed; the limit `-1` keeps them (6). A leading separator produces a leading empty string (`" x y ".split(" ")` gives `["", "x", "", "y"]`). Prefer `split("\\s+")` after `strip()` for whitespace.

#### Passwords and char arrays

Because a `String` is immutable, a password held in one stays in memory until garbage collection, and may be visible in a heap dump or in the string pool if it came from a literal. Security-sensitive APIs (`KeyStore.load`, `PBEKeySpec`, `Console.readPassword`) therefore take `char[]`, which you can overwrite with `Arrays.fill(pw, '\0')` as soon as you are done (the last printed `0` above is the code of that overwritten character). This is a mitigation, not a guarantee: the framework that read the password from an HTTP request has often already made `String` copies. Still, never log a password and never keep one in a field longer than necessary.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Use `isBlank()` to test for empty or whitespace-only text and `strip()` (not `trim()`) to remove whitespace; `strip` understands Unicode white space, `trim` only removes characters up to U+0020. Compare with a constant first to avoid null checks: `"yes".equals(answer)` never throws when `answer` is `null`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A `String` is immutable; "modifying" methods return new objects, so always use their return value.

- Since Java 9 a `String` stores a `byte[]` plus a `coder` (Latin-1 or UTF-16), so ASCII text costs one byte per char.
- Literals and compile-time constants are pooled; `new String(...)` and run-time concatenation are not. Compare content with `equals`, never `==`.
- `+` compiles to `invokedynamic` (`StringConcatFactory`) since Java 9; inside loops use `StringBuilder` to avoid quadratic copying.
- Prefer `strip` over `trim`, `StringBuilder` over `StringBuffer`; remember that `split` takes a regex and drops trailing empties.

Strings are rarely built by hand. Reports need aligned columns and two decimals; input needs to be validated and pulled apart; multi-line text (JSON, SQL, HTML) needs to sit in source code without a thicket of escapes. Java has a format mini-language (`printf`), a regular-expression engine (`java.util.regex`), and text blocks for exactly these jobs. This chapter shows each, with the traps that cost people hours.

### Formatting with printf and Formatter

`String.format`, `System.out.printf`, `PrintStream.format`, `String.formatted` (Java 15) and `java.util.Formatter` all share one syntax: a format string with specifiers of the form `%[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion`. Each specifier consumes one argument (unless you give an index such as `%2$s`).

blocks.caption: The conversions you will use most.

blocks.text: Flags and width tune the layout: `-` left-justify, `0` pad with zeros, `+` always show a sign, `,` group digits, `(` negative numbers in parentheses, `#` alternate form. Width is the minimum field width; precision after the dot means decimals for `%f` and a maximum length for `%s`.

blocks.title: Fmt.java

blocks.code:
$ java Fmt.java
[   42] [42   ] [00042] [1,234,567] [+42]
[   3.142] [3] [1.234568e+04] [9,876,543.22]
[java] [      java] [java      ] [jav] [JAVA]
[ff] [FF] [10] [00003.14] [true] [J] [%]
b a b
1.234.567,89
1,234,567.89
0.13 0.14 1 2
java.util.IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double
one java.util.MissingFormatArgumentException: Format specifier '%s'
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- **Locale matters.** Without an explicit `Locale`, `format` uses the default locale of the JVM (`Locale.getDefault(Locale.Category.FORMAT)`), so the same code prints `1.234.567,89` on a German machine. For machine-readable output (files, JSON, logs parsed by tools) pass `Locale.ROOT` or `Locale.US`.
- **Rounding is HALF\_UP**, not banker's rounding: `0.125` prints `0.13`, `2.5` with `%.0f` gives `3`. It rounds the decimal expansion of the binary double, which is why `0.135` (really 0.13500000000000000888...) gives `0.14`. Money does not belong in `double`; see the chapter on BigDecimal.
- **Wrong arguments fail at run time**, not compile time: `%d` with a double throws `IllegalFormatConversionException`, too few arguments throw `MissingFormatArgumentException` (note the partial output `one` was already written). IDE inspections and `-Xlint` do not catch all of these.
- Use `%n`, not `\n`, in `printf` strings for portable line endings.

`Formatter` itself is a class that writes formatted text to any `Appendable` (a `StringBuilder`, a file, a `PrintStream`). You rarely instantiate it, but it explains why `String.format` is relatively slow: each call parses the format string. In a hot loop prefer building with `StringBuilder`; elsewhere, readability wins.

### Regular expressions

A **regular expression** (regex) is a compact pattern describing a set of strings. Java's engine lives in `java.util.regex` and has two main classes: `Pattern` (a compiled regex, immutable and thread-safe) and `Matcher` (the state of one match attempt on one input, not thread-safe). Compiling is expensive, so keep a `Pattern` in a `static final` field instead of calling `String.matches` or `replaceAll` in a loop (they compile the pattern every time).

#### The syntax you need

- Character classes: `[abc]`, `[a-z]`, `[^0-9]` (negation); shortcuts `\d` digit, `\w` word char, `\s` whitespace, `.` any char except line end. In a Java string literal every backslash is doubled: `"\\d+"`.
- Quantifiers: `*` zero or more, `+` one or more, `?` optional, `{n}`, `{n,m}`.
- Anchors: `^` start, `$` end, `\b` word boundary.
- Groups: `( ... )` captures, `(?: ... )` does not capture, `(?<name> ... )` captures with a name; `|` alternation.
- Flags: `Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE` or inline `(?i)`; `MULTILINE`, `DOTALL`, `UNICODE_CASE`.

#### Matching, finding and groups

There are three ways to apply a matcher, and mixing them up is a common bug: `matches()` requires the whole input to match, `lookingAt()` requires a match at the start only, and `find()` searches for the next match anywhere (call it in a loop).

blocks.title: Rx.java

blocks.code:
$ java Rx.java
2026-10-09 year=2026 month=10 at 4-14
2026-10-12 year=2026 month=10 at 21-31
false true
#
#bold# and #italic#
Smith, John
a<1>b<2>c<3>
[a, b, c]
a-b --- \Qa.b\E
2 null
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- **Group numbering** counts opening parentheses from left to right; group 0 is the whole match. Named groups also have numbers. A group that did not participate (`(b)?` above) returns `null`, not an empty string.
- **Greedy versus lazy.** `<.+>` is greedy: it grabs as much as possible, so the whole input from the first `<` to the last `>` became one `#`. Appending `?` (`<.+?>`) makes the quantifier lazy: it takes as little as possible, giving two tags per match. Possessive quantifiers (`.++`) never give back characters, which makes failures fast when you know backtracking cannot help.
- `replaceAll` **replacement syntax.** `$1`, `$2` refer to groups; a literal `$` or `\` in the replacement must be escaped, or use `Matcher.quoteReplacement`. The lambda form (`replaceAll(Function<MatchResult,String>)`, Java 9) avoids that problem entirely.
- `replace` **is literal,** `replaceAll` **is regex.** `"a.b".replaceAll(".", "-")` replaced every character. `Pattern.quote` wraps text so it is matched literally.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not parse HTML, XML, JSON or nested structures with regex. Regular expressions cannot count nesting. Use a real parser; reserve regex for flat patterns such as ids, dates and log lines.

### Catastrophic backtracking

Java's engine is a **backtracking** matcher: when a path fails, it returns to the last choice point and tries another. If a pattern contains nested or overlapping repetition, the number of paths can grow exponentially with input length. One bad pattern on a user-supplied string can pin a CPU core for minutes. This is the **ReDoS** (regular-expression denial of service) vulnerability, and it has caused real outages.

The JDK has optimisations for some nested-group cases, so some textbook examples such as `(a+)+b` no longer explode here. The following still does. The pattern `(a?)` repeated n times followed by n times `a` can match the n-letter input only by choosing "empty" for every optional, and the engine tries all 2 to the power n combinations first.

blocks.title: Backtrack.java

blocks.code:
$ java Backtrack.java
n=14  nested optionals: 70 ms   a{n}: 0 ms
n=16  nested optionals: 116 ms   a{n}: 0 ms
n=18  nested optionals: 430 ms   a{n}: 0 ms
n=20  nested optionals: 645 ms   a{n}: 0 ms
n=22  nested optionals: 1090 ms   a{n}: 0 ms
blocks.title: Typical output (measured on the build machine; timings vary run to run)

blocks.text:
Growth is clearly super-linear; in our extra runs n=26 took several seconds. Real-world culprits look like `(\w+\s?)*$` or `(.*a){12}`, usually written by someone validating an e-mail address or a URL. Defences:

1. Avoid nested quantifiers over the same characters; rewrite the pattern so each input char can be matched in only one way.
2. Use possessive quantifiers (`++`, `*+`) or atomic groups `(?>...)` when backtracking is pointless.
3. Limit input length before matching, and run regex on untrusted input with a timeout (for example in a worker whose result you abandon) because `Matcher` offers no built-in time limit. A custom `CharSequence` that checks a deadline in `charAt` is a known trick.
4. For fixed formats prefer plain parsing (`split`, `indexOf`, `LocalDate.parse`) over a clever regex.

### Text blocks

Before Java 15, multi-line text meant `"...\n" +` on every line and escaped quotes. A **text block** (Java 15, JEP 378) starts with three double quotes followed by a line break and ends with three double quotes. The compiler strips the **incidental indentation**: the common leading whitespace of all lines, including the closing delimiter's line, is removed, so you can indent the block to match your code.

blocks.title: Tok.java

blocks.code:
$ java Tok.java
{
  "name": "Asha",
  "tags": ["a", "b"]
}
one line
  indented "quotes"      tab
end
3
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text: The rules in short: double quotes need no escaping; a trailing `\` joins lines (no newline); `\t`, `\n` and other escapes still work; `\s` (Java 15) keeps a trailing space that would otherwise be stripped; the text ends with a newline only if the closing delimiter is on its own line (compare `json` with `t`). Trailing spaces on each line are removed. For templating use `formatted(...)`: `"""Hello %s""".formatted(name)`. String templates were previewed in Java 21 to 23 but withdrawn, so do not plan on them.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Put the closing `"""` on its own line, aligned with the code you want as column 0. Moving it left adds indentation to every line; moving it right changes nothing, because the smallest indent wins.

### StringTokenizer and split pitfalls

`StringTokenizer` is a legacy class (its Javadoc says new code should use `split` or the regex package). Notice in the last listing that it counted 3 tokens in `"a,b,,c"`: it silently skips empty tokens, whereas `split(",")` keeps the middle empty string. Use `String.split` for simple cases and `Scanner` when you need typed tokens (`nextInt`, `nextDouble`) from a stream.

`split` has the pitfalls we already met: the delimiter is a regex (`split("|")` splits between every char, `split("\\|")` is what you meant); trailing empties are removed; a leading empty string is produced when the input starts with a delimiter (Java 8+ drops it only for a zero-width match at the start); `split(regex, limit)` caps the number of parts, and a negative limit keeps everything. When performance matters and the delimiter is a single non-special char, `split` takes a fast path that avoids the regex engine.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between greedy, lazy and possessive quantifiers? Greedy (`.*`) matches as much as possible and backs off one character at a time if the rest fails. Lazy (`.*?`) matches as little as possible and expands as needed. Possessive (`.*+`) matches as much as possible and never backs off, so it fails fast but can miss matches that greedy would find.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Validation of request fields in Spring (`@Pattern(regexp = "...")` from Bean Validation) compiles and runs exactly this `java.util.regex` engine on user input. A badly written regexp in an annotation is a ReDoS hole in a public endpoint: review those patterns as carefully as SQL.

### More regex: named groups, lookahead, flags and replacement

The earlier examples used numbered groups. Real patterns grow, and numbers become fragile when you add a group in the middle; use **named groups** `(?<name>...)` and read them with `group("name")`. The next program also shows replacement with back-references (`$1`), a replacement computed by a function, a lookahead, flags, and the quoting helpers.

blocks.title: Rx2.java

blocks.code:
$ java Rx2.java
15/08/2025 at 4-14
01/09/2025 at 21-31
15.08.2025
a<1>b<2>c<3>
price: 100 USD, *** EUR
true
true
true
false true
\Q1+1\E two=2
a\$b
3
2
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `find()` scans for the next match and `start()`/`end()` give its position; `matches()` demands that the whole input match, `lookingAt()` only the beginning.
- In a replacement string `$3` means "group 3", and a literal `$` or backslash must be escaped. When the replacement text comes from user input, wrap it in `Matcher.quoteReplacement`; when the pattern text comes from user input, wrap it in `Pattern.quote` (which produces `\Q...\E`). Otherwise `"1+1"` is read as a regex and fails to match.
- `replaceAll(Function<MatchResult,String>)` (Java 9) computes each replacement in code, which is clearer than a trick with groups.
- The **lookahead** `(?=...)` checks what follows without consuming it: `\\d+(?= EUR)` matches the number before " EUR" only. Likewise `(?!...)` (negative lookahead) and `(?<=...)` / `(?<!...)` (lookbehind). The password check `(?=.*\\d)(?=.*[a-z]).{8,}` chains two lookaheads from the same start position: "contains a digit" and "contains a lowercase letter", then at least 8 characters.
- Flags: `CASE_INSENSITIVE`, `MULTILINE` (`^` and `$` match at line breaks; the `a\nb` example finds `^b`), `DOTALL` (`.` matches line breaks; without it `a.c` does not match `a`, newline, `c`), and `UNICODE_CASE`. Inline forms such as `(?i)` work inside the pattern.
- `\\p{Lu}` and `\\p{L}` are Unicode categories (uppercase letter, any letter), so `\\p{Lu}\\p{L}*` counts the words "Émile" and "Zoé" correctly where `[A-Z]` would not. Use `matcher.results()` (Java 9) for a stream of matches.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: A `Pattern` is immutable and thread-safe, while a `Matcher` is not. Compile patterns once into `private static final` `Pattern` fields; `String.matches`, `replaceAll` and `split` (for multi-character patterns) recompile on every call, which is a measurable cost in hot paths. Prefer a plain `String.replace(CharSequence, CharSequence)` when you do not need a regex at all.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
`printf` formats are checked only at run time; always pass a `Locale` for machine-readable output, and note rounding is HALF\_UP.

- A `Pattern` is compiled once and shared; a `Matcher` is per use. `matches` needs the whole input, `find` scans.
- Quantifiers are greedy by default; `?` makes them lazy, `+` possessive. `replace` is literal, `replaceAll` and `split` use regex.
- Nested quantifiers on untrusted input can cause catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS); simplify the pattern and cap input size.
- Text blocks strip incidental indentation, need no quote escaping, and end with a newline only if the delimiter is on its own line.

"It works on my machine" is often an encoding or locale problem. The text `café` turns into `cafÃ©`, an emoji "has length 2", a Turkish user cannot log in because `"I".toLowerCase()` produced the wrong letter, and a German server prints `1.234,5` into a file that a US parser rejects. These bugs share one cause: confusing characters, code points, bytes, and cultural conventions. This chapter separates the four layers so you can reason about each.

### Characters, code points and bytes

**Unicode** assigns every character in every writing system a number called a **code point**, written `U+0041` for `A` or `U+1F600` for the grinning-face emoji. Code points run from U+0000 to U+10FFFF. Unicode itself says nothing about bytes; an **encoding** maps code points to bytes:

- **UTF-8**: 1 to 4 bytes per code point; ASCII stays one byte. The dominant encoding of files, the web, JSON, and databases.
- **UTF-16**: 2 bytes for code points up to U+FFFF (the Basic Multilingual Plane, BMP), 4 bytes (a **surrogate pair** of two 16-bit units) above that. This is how Java represents text in memory.
- **ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1)** and **US-ASCII**: legacy single-byte sets that can represent only a few hundred or 128 characters.

Java's `char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, not a "character". `String.length()` counts those units. For text inside the BMP the two coincide; for emoji, many historic scripts and some CJK extensions they do not.

blocks.title: Uni.java

blocks.code:
$ java Uni.java
length()       = 5
codePointCount = 4
char 0: U+0041  surrogate=false
char 1: U+00E9  surrogate=false
char 2: U+20AC  surrogate=false
char 3: U+D83D  surrogate=true
char 4: U+DE00  surrogate=true
cp U+41  LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A
cp U+E9  LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE
cp U+20AC  EURO SIGN
cp U+1F600  GRINNING FACE
ISO-8859-1 -> 4 bytes 41e93f3f
UTF-8 -> 10 bytes 41c3a9e282acf09f9880
UTF-16BE -> 10 bytes 004100e920acd83dde00
UTF-16 -> 12 bytes feff004100e920acd83dde00
5 bytes, wrong decode has 5 chars, right decode equals original: true
false 1 2 true
default charset = UTF-8
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- Four code points but `length()` is 5: the emoji is stored as the surrogate pair `D83D DE00`. Looping with `charAt` would visit the two halves separately; `codePoints()`, `codePointAt`, and `codePointCount` work on whole code points. `new` `StringBuilder(s).reverse()` is surrogate-aware (it keeps pairs intact), but `char[]` reversal by hand is not.
- The same text takes 4, 10, 10, or 12 bytes depending on the charset. `UTF-16` (without BE/LE) writes a 2-byte byte-order mark `feff` first. In ISO-8859-1 the characters it cannot represent became `3f`, the question mark. Silent replacement is the default behaviour of `getBytes`; for strict handling use `CharsetEncoder` with `CodingErrorAction.REPORT`.
- Decoding UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 does not fail; it produces garbage of the wrong length (the "mojibake" `cafÃ©`). Encoding and decoding must use the same charset.
- `é` can be one code point or `e` plus a combining accent. They look identical but `equals` is false. Normalise with `java.text.Normalizer` (NFC) before comparing, hashing or storing user-visible text such as usernames.

#### Always name the charset

Since Java 18 (JEP 400) the default charset is UTF-8 on every platform, so `new String(bytes)` and `Files.readString(path)` are less dangerous than they were. The old platform charset is still available as the system property `native.encoding`, and it still controls what the console (`System.out`) uses; on the build machine `native.encoding` and `stdout.encoding` are `ANSI_X3.4-1968` (plain ASCII), so non-ASCII output printed as `?` here. That is a terminal problem, not a Java problem. Good habits regardless of version:

- Pass `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly to `getBytes`, `new String`, `InputStreamReader`, `FileReader` (Java 11+ has a charset constructor), `Files.readString` and `Files.writeString`.
- Set `Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8` (or rely on the framework default of UTF-8) for HTTP.
- Check the encoding of the database connection and of source files (`javac -encoding UTF-8`; UTF-8 is the default from Java 18, but build tools may set their own).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `String.getBytes()` without arguments uses the default charset. Before Java 18 that was whatever the OS said (`windows-1252`, `ANSI_X3.4-1968`, ...), which is why the same program produced different files on different machines. Never use the no-argument forms in new code.

### Locale: culture-sensitive behaviour

A `java.util.Locale` identifies a language and optionally a region (`en-US`, `de-DE`, `hi-IN`). Many JDK methods consult a locale: `String.format`, `toUpperCase`, `NumberFormat`, `DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate`, `Collator`. The JVM chooses a default from the OS (`Locale.getDefault()`); servers often run in a different locale from developer laptops, so locale-dependent code that was never tested outside your locale is a source of bugs.

Create locales with `Locale.forLanguageTag("en-IN")` or the constants (`Locale.US`, `Locale.GERMANY`). The `Locale` constructors are deprecated since Java 19. `Locale.ROOT` means "no particular locale"; it is what you want for protocol identifiers, keys and anything a program (not a person) reads.

blocks.title: Loc.java

blocks.code:
$ java Loc.java
t\u0131tle T\u0130TLE
title TITLE
STRASSE
en-US  1,234,567.891  $1,234,567.89
de-DE  1.234.567,891  1.234.567,89\u00a0\u20ac
en-IN  1,234,567.891  \u20b91,234,567.89
1234.5 1234.5 12
[Zoo, apple, zebra, \u00e4pfel]
[\u00e4pfel, apple, zebra, Zoo]
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### The Turkish i

Turkish has two letters i: dotted (`i`/`İ`) and dotless (`ı`/`I`). With a Turkish locale, `"TITLE".toLowerCase()` yields `tıtle` (a dotless ı) and `"title".toUpperCase()` yields `TİTLE`, so `"FILE".toLowerCase().equals("file")` is false on a Turkish machine. This has broken file-extension checks, SQL keyword matching and HTTP header handling in real products. The fix: for identifiers, enum names, protocol tokens and map keys always write `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` or `toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)`. Note also that upper-casing can change length (`straße` becomes `STRASSE`), so case conversion is not a 1:1 mapping.

#### NumberFormat, parsing and sorting

`NumberFormat` gives locale-correct output: separators (`1.234.567,891` in Germany), currency symbols and placement (`1.234.567,89 €` with a no-break space, ), and in India `₹`. Other factories: `getPercentInstance`, `getIntegerInstance`, `getCompactNumberInstance` (Java 12; prints `1M`). `NumberFormat` is not thread-safe: do not share one instance between threads.

Parsing has a trap shown on the `1234.5 1234.5 12` line: `parse` stops at the first character it cannot use and returns what it has, so `"12abc"` parses as 12 with no error. Use `parse(String, ParsePosition)` and check that the whole input was consumed if you need strictness. And `Double.parseDouble` always expects `.` as the decimal point regardless of locale.

Plain `String` ordering (`compareTo`) compares UTF-16 code units, so accented letters sort after `z`. For user-visible lists use `java.text.Collator` for the user's locale, as the last two lines show: in German collation `äpfel` sorts before `apple`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Money amounts should not be formatted with `double` and then parsed back. Format with `NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance` (or `DecimalFormat` with explicit `RoundingMode`) for display only, and store amounts as `BigDecimal` or integer cents. The next chapter covers `BigDecimal`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between a `char`, a code point and a byte in Java? A `char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. A code point is a Unicode number (up to U+10FFFF); code points above U+FFFF need two `char`s (a surrogate pair). A byte only exists once text is encoded with a charset such as UTF-8. So `length()` counts code units, `codePointCount` counts characters in the Unicode sense, and `getBytes(cs).length` counts bytes.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Boot serialises JSON as UTF-8 and parses request bodies using the declared charset, but it uses the JVM default locale for things like `@DateTimeFormat` and message bundles unless you configure `LocaleResolver`/`Accept-Language` handling. Docker images often run with the `POSIX`/`C` locale, which is another reason to write `Locale.ROOT` for machine-readable formatting.

### Normalization, Base64 and hex: text versus bytes

Two more everyday tools sit between text and bytes. **Normalization** deals with the fact that the same visible text can be encoded in several ways. **Base64** and **hex** are encodings that turn arbitrary bytes into safe ASCII text; they are not encryption.

blocks.title: Nz.java

blocks.code:
$ java Nz.java
false 1 2
true
Cafe naive
SGkgw6k/ -_8
486920c3a93f 48:69:20:C3:A9:3F
true 5
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
- `é` can be one code point (U+00E9, "composed") or `e` followed by a combining acute accent (U+0301, "decomposed"). They print identically but `equals` says `false` (lengths 1 and 2). `Normalizer.Form.NFC` composes, `NFD` decomposes; normalise to NFC before comparing, hashing or storing user-supplied text such as usernames.
- NFD followed by removing combining marks (`\\p{M}`) is a common way to strip accents for search or slugs: `Café` `naïve` becomes `Cafe naive`.
- `java.util.Base64` has three flavours: basic (`+` and `/`, padded with `=`), URL-safe (`-` and `_`, used in JWTs and URLs; add `withoutPadding()` to drop the `=`) and MIME (line-wrapped). The string `Hi é?` is 6 bytes in UTF-8 and becomes 8 Base64 characters. Always convert text to bytes with an explicit charset before encoding.
- `HexFormat` (Java 17) formats and parses hexadecimal with optional delimiters and case. Before it you had to write `String.format("%02x", b)` loops.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Base64 is an encoding, not protection. Anyone can decode `SGkgw6k/`. Do not use it to hide passwords or tokens; use hashing (for passwords, with a slow salted algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2 through a library) or encryption.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A `char` is a UTF-16 code unit; a code point may need two. Use `codePoints()` and `codePointCount` when characters outside the BMP matter.

- Encoding and decoding must use the same charset; always pass `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly. Java 18+ defaults to UTF-8.
- Normalise (`Normalizer` NFC) before comparing user text; use `Collator` to sort for humans.
- Case conversion and number formatting depend on `Locale`; use `Locale.ROOT` for identifiers and protocol data.
- `NumberFormat` is locale-aware, not thread-safe, and its `parse` can stop early without an error.

Primitive `int`, `long` and `double` are fast and fine for most arithmetic, but they have three hard limits. They overflow silently (`Long.MAX_VALUE + 1` wraps to a negative number), they cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly (`0.1` `+ 0.2` is not `0.3`), and they have a fixed size. This chapter covers the tools for the cases where those limits matter: `BigDecimal` for exact decimal arithmetic (money, rates, measurements), `BigInteger` for integers of any size, the `Math` class for everything in between, and the random-number and identifier classes you will meet in real programs.

### Why double is wrong for money

A `double` stores a binary fraction: a sign, an exponent and 52 bits of mantissa. A number like 0.1 has no finite binary expansion (just as 1/3 has no finite decimal expansion), so the stored value is the nearest binary fraction. Add a few such values and the tiny errors become visible. The chapter on type conversion in Part 2 showed `0.1 + 0.2`; here is what is actually stored for 0.1, and the fix.

blocks.title: Bd.java

blocks.code:
$ java Bd.java
0.30000000000000004
0.3
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
0.1
false 0 621 6202
scale=2 precision=3 unscaled=200
59.97 scale 2
4.49775 -> 4.50
Non-terminating decimal expansion; no exact representable decimal result.
0.33333
0.3333333
1.1 1E+2 100
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `new BigDecimal(0.1)` takes the already-wrong `double` and exposes its exact value (0.1000000000000000055511...). Use the `String` constructor, or `BigDecimal.valueOf(double)`, which goes through `Double.toString` and so gives `0.1`.
- A `BigDecimal` is an unscaled integer plus a **scale** (the number of digits after the decimal point). `2.00` is unscaled 200, scale 2. Multiplying adds the scales: `19.99 × 3` has scale 2 + 0.
- `equals` compares value **and** scale, so `2.0` and `2.00` are not equal and have different hash codes. `compareTo` compares numeric value only. This matters for `HashMap` keys and `HashSet`: use `compareTo` for numeric equality, or normalise the scale with `setScale` first.
- `divide` without a rounding instruction throws `ArithmeticException` when the exact quotient has infinitely many digits. Always say how to round: give a scale and a `RoundingMode`, or a `MathContext`.
- `BigDecimal` is immutable. `price.add(x)` returns a new object; ignoring the result is a classic bug (the same trap as `String`).

### Scale, precision and rounding modes

Three words are easy to mix up. The **scale** counts digits right of the decimal point (it can be negative: `1E+2` has scale -2). The **precision** counts all significant digits of the unscaled value (`2.00` has precision 3). A `MathContext` bundles a precision and a `RoundingMode`; `MathContext.DECIMAL32`, `DECIMAL64` and `DECIMAL128` mirror the IEEE 754 decimal formats (7, 16 and 34 digits). Use `setScale(n, mode)` when you care about digits after the point (money: scale 2), and `round(MathContext)` or `divide(x, mc)` when you care about significant digits (scientific values).

Java defines eight rounding modes in `java.math.RoundingMode`. The table below was produced by calling `new` `BigDecimal(s).setScale(0, mode)` for each input; read it column by column, noticing what each mode does to the halves (2.5, -2.5) and to negative numbers.

blocks.title: Rm.java

blocks.text: `UP` rounds away from zero and `DOWN` towards zero (truncation); `CEILING` and `FLOOR` round towards positive and negative infinity, so they differ from `UP`/`DOWN` only for negatives. The three `HALF_` modes differ only on exact ties (the `.5` columns): `HALF_UP` is the "school" rule (and the one `printf` uses), `HALF_DOWN` the opposite, and `HALF_EVEN`, also called banker's rounding, sends ties to the even neighbour (2.5 → 2, 5.5 → 6, 3.5 → 4). Over many operations `HALF_EVEN` has no systematic upward bias, which is why accounting standards and IEEE 754 prefer it. The ninth value, `UNNECESSARY`, asserts that no rounding is needed and throws `ArithmeticException` if it is.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `Math.round(-2.5)` returns `-2` (it rounds half towards positive infinity), while `BigDecimal HALF_UP` turns -2.5 into -3. `Math.rint(2.5)` is `2.0` (half-even). Three rounding rules with similar names exist in one language, so write the mode down explicitly whenever the result is a bill.

#### Practical rules for money

- Store money as `BigDecimal` with an agreed scale (or as `long` minor units such as cents; many payment APIs do this). Never as `double`.
- Create from `String` or `valueOf`, never `new BigDecimal(double)`.
- Round once, at the end of a calculation or at a defined business step, with an explicit `RoundingMode`.
- Compare with `compareTo`; use `signum()` for "is it positive, zero or negative".
- Do not use `stripTrailingZeros()` for display without `toPlainString()`: `new` `BigDecimal("100").stripTrailingZeros()` prints `1E+2`.
- JSON, JDBC and Spring map `NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` columns to `BigDecimal` naturally; keep the type end to end.
- `BigDecimal` is much slower than `double` (it allocates objects). Use it where exactness matters, not for physics simulations.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why shouldn't you use `double` for money, and what do you use instead? A `double` is a binary floating-point value; most decimal fractions such as 0.10 cannot be represented exactly, and errors accumulate and make totals off by a cent. Use `BigDecimal` (constructed from a `String`, with an explicit scale and `RoundingMode`) or integer minor units. Mention that `equals` on `BigDecimal` compares scale too, so use `compareTo`.

### BigInteger: integers without a ceiling

`java.math.BigInteger` represents an integer of arbitrary size, limited only by memory. It is immutable, has no operators (you call `add`, `multiply`, `pow`, `mod`, `gcd`), and has number-theory helpers such as `modPow`, `modInverse` and `isProbablePrime`. It is what cryptography code, factorials and exact combinatorics use.

blocks.title: Bi.java

blocks.text:
`25!` already needs 84 bits, so it cannot fit in a `long` (63 bits of magnitude). The number `2^127 - 1` is a Mersenne prime; `isProbablePrime(50)` runs Miller-Rabin style tests with an error probability below 2^-50. Convert back to primitives with the `*Exact` methods (`longValueExact`, `intValueExact`), which throw instead of silently truncating like `longValue()`. `BigInteger` multiplication switches algorithm with size (schoolbook, Karatsuba, Toom-Cook), so it is fast for hundreds of digits but not free; the last line shows that a plain `long` just wraps.

### The Math class and exact arithmetic

`java.lang.Math` holds static numeric helpers. Most are thin wrappers over hardware instructions or intrinsics. The ones worth knowing, with traps, are in the run below.

blocks.title: Mth.java

blocks.code:
$ java Mth.java
3 -2 4 2.0 4.0
-4 -3 1 -1
-2147483648
Overflow to represent absolute value of Integer.MIN_VALUE
integer overflow
5.0 3.0 1024.0 NaN 10
4 7.0
2.220446049250313E-16 1.0000000000000002
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
- `Math.floorDiv` and `floorMod` round towards negative infinity. Java's `/` and `%` truncate towards zero, so `-7 % 2` is `-1`. For array indices wrapped around a ring buffer (`index % size` when index may be negative) use `floorMod`. (`Math.floorMod(x, n)` is always in `0..n-1` for positive `n`.)
- `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` returns `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, still negative, because +2147483648 does not fit. This even breaks the classic `Math.abs(hash) % n` bucket-picking code when `hash` happens to be `MIN_VALUE`. Use `floorMod(hash, n)`.
- The `*Exact` family (`addExact`, `subtractExact`, `multiplyExact`, `incrementExact`, `negateExact`, `toIntExact`, `absExact` since 15) throws `ArithmeticException` on overflow instead of wrapping. Use them wherever silent wrap-around would be a bug (balances, quantities, sizes).
- `Math.clamp(value, min, max)` is new in Java 21; `ceilDiv` since 18; `fma` (fused multiply-add) computes `a*b+c` with a single rounding.
- `Math.sqrt(-1)` is `NaN`, no exception. Floating-point failures are values, not errors (see the NaN discussion in Part 2).
- `Math.ulp(x)` is the gap between `x` and the next representable `double`: for 1.0 it is about 2.2e-16, which explains why comparing doubles with `==` is fragile.

#### Math versus StrictMath

`StrictMath` guarantees bit-for-bit identical results on every platform by using the fdlibm algorithms. `Math` is allowed a few ulps of error for `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow` and so on, so the JIT can use faster hardware instructions. Since Java 17 (JEP 306) all floating-point arithmetic is strict (`strictfp` is redundant and gives a warning), but the transcendental functions in `Math` are still allowed to differ slightly from `StrictMath`. Use `StrictMath` only if you need reproducible results across machines, for example in a test oracle or a game simulation synchronised between clients.

### Random numbers: Random, ThreadLocalRandom, SecureRandom

Which random class you pick is a design decision, not a detail.

blocks.text: Two `Random` objects with the same seed produce the same sequence: that is the point of a pseudo-random generator (a deterministic algorithm that looks random), and it is why `Random` is wrong for secrets. `Random` is a 48-bit linear congruential generator, so anyone who sees a few outputs can predict the rest. Java 17 added `java.util.random.RandomGenerator` (JEP 356), a common interface implemented by `Random`, `ThreadLocalRandom`, `SecureRandom` and the new families such as `L64X128MixRandom` (shown above, which has good statistical quality and supports splitting for parallel streams). `RandomGenerator.getDefault()` returns a recommended general-purpose generator (`L32X64MixRandom` on this JDK).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never use `Random` or `Math.random()` for passwords, tokens, reset links or anything an attacker benefits from guessing. Use `SecureRandom` (and `new SecureRandom()` is thread-safe; reuse one instance). Another classic mistake: `new` `Random()` inside a loop or per request. Create one instance and reuse it, or use `ThreadLocalRandom.current()`.

#### UUID

A `java.util.UUID` is a 128-bit identifier, written as 36 characters (`8-4-4-4-12` hex digits). `UUID.randomUUID()` creates a version 4 UUID from `SecureRandom`: 122 random bits, so collisions are, for practical purposes, impossible. The version digit is the first character of the third group (the 15th character, index 14: `4` above). `UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes` creates a version 3 (MD5, name-based) UUID, which is deterministic: the same input always yields the same UUID, useful for derived ids. The JDK has no built-in generator for version 7 (time-ordered) UUIDs, to my knowledge; if you need index-friendly ids in a database, use a library or a separate id scheme, because random v4 values scatter inserts across a B-tree index.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Data and JPA entities often use `UUID` primary keys; remember they are 16 bytes in a native `uuid` column, but 36 characters if stored as `varchar`. For one-time tokens in a Spring Security flow, generate them with `SecureRandom` bytes encoded using `Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Use `BigDecimal` (built from `String` or `valueOf`) with an explicit `RoundingMode` for money; compare with `compareTo`, not `equals`.

- `BigInteger` removes the size limit of `long`; convert back with the `*Exact` methods so overflow is an error, not a surprise.
- `Math.floorMod`, `Math.absExact` and the `*Exact` methods avoid the silent traps of `%`, `abs` and `+` on primitives.
- `Random` is predictable, `ThreadLocalRandom` is fast in threads, `SecureRandom` is for secrets.
- A random `UUID` (v4) is a good unique id, but not a secret token and not index-friendly.

Time looks simple until you ship software to more than one place. "Midnight" depends on a time zone, a day is sometimes 23 or 25 hours long, February has 28 or 29 days, and a month is not a fixed number of days. Java's `java.time` package (added in Java 8, JSR 310) models these facts with separate types for separate ideas. Learning which type means what is most of the work.

### Why Date and Calendar failed

Before Java 8 you had `java.util.Date` and `java.util.Calendar`. Both are still in the JDK, and you will meet them in legacy code and in older libraries, so you must recognise their problems. The program below shows several of them. It is run with the default zone set to UTC so the output is reproducible.

blocks.title: Old.java

blocks.text:
What went wrong in the first three lines: `new Date(2024, 1, 31)` takes the year as an offset from 1900 (so the year is 3924) and months from 0 (so 1 means February), and February 31 silently rolls over to March 2. `GregorianCalendar` also counts months from 0 (`MONTH` is 2 for what a human calls March, after the roll-over). `SimpleDateFormat` is lenient by default and happily turned "2025-13-45" into 14 February 2026. In addition:

- `Date` and `Calendar` are mutable, so passing one around invites defensive copies and bugs; `SimpleDateFormat` is mutable *and* not thread-safe, so a shared static instance corrupts output under load.
- `Date` is really an instant (milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z) that prints in the default zone, which confuses people into thinking it holds a zone.
- There is no type for "just a date" or "just a time"; `java.sql.Date` is a subclass that pretends to be one.

The `java.time` types fix all of these: they are immutable (so thread-safe), months are 1 to 12, invalid dates throw, each type represents one concept, and the formatter is thread-safe. Convert at the edges with `Date.toInstant()`, `Date.from(instant)`, `java.sql.Date.valueOf(localDate)` and `GregorianCalendar.toZonedDateTime()`.

blocks.text: Think of two worlds. The first is **machine time**: a single point on the timeline, with no calendar and no zone. `Instant` is that. The second is **human time**: the fields on a wall clock or calendar, which mean nothing until you say where. `LocalDate`, `LocalTime` and `LocalDateTime` are human time without a place; `ZonedDateTime` and `OffsetDateTime` are human time pinned to a place, so they correspond to exactly one instant.

blocks.title: T1.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `plusMonths(1)` on 31 January gives 29 February: when the target day does not exist, `java.time` clamps to the last valid day instead of rolling over like `Calendar`. Every `java.time` object is immutable, so `d.plusMonths(1)` returns a new `LocalDate` and `d` stays `2024-01-31`.
- `TemporalAdjusters` express calendar logic ("last day of month", "next Monday") without hand-written loops.
- The `Instant 1700000000` is a single moment. The same moment is 17:13 in New York (UTC-5 in November) and 03:43 the next day in Kolkata (+05:30). `equals` on the two `Instant`s is true. Compare `ZonedDateTime`s through `toInstant()` or `isBefore`/`isAfter`.
- `Period` is calendar-based (years, months, days). `Duration` is exact time-based (hours, minutes, seconds). Calling `Duration.between` on two `LocalDate`s throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException` because dates have no time-of-day; use `Period.between` or `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`.
- The `PT9H30M30S` and `P4Y15D` strings are ISO 8601 duration syntax (`P` period, `T` time part).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Why `Instant.toString()` ends in `Z`: it is ISO 8601 for UTC ("Zulu"). An `Instant` has no zone; it is printed in UTC. Call `atZone(zoneId)` to view it in another zone, and use `ZoneId.of("Region/City")`, never abbreviations like "IST" which are ambiguous.

### Formatting and parsing with DateTimeFormatter

`DateTimeFormatter` is immutable and thread-safe, so keep formatters in `static final` fields. There are three ways to get one: the predefined ISO constants (`ISO_LOCAL_DATE`, `ISO_INSTANT`, `ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME`), localized styles (`ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM)`) and pattern strings via `ofPattern`.

rows: month number / short name / full name

blocks.text:
The usual mistakes are `mm` (minutes) vs `MM` (months), `hh` vs `HH`, and `yyyy` vs `YYYY` (week-based year, which gives the wrong year around 31 December; never use `YYYY` unless you mean it). For names of months and days always pass a `Locale` so the output does not depend on the server.

Parsing has a subtle default called the **resolver style**. The default, `SMART`, repairs impossible values; `STRICT` rejects them; `LENIENT` rolls them over. The next program shows the effect of `31/04/2025`.

blocks.title: DateFmt.java

blocks.code:
$ java DateFmt.java
31 Jan 2024, 09:30 | 2024-01-31
2025-08-15
2025-04-30
Text '31/04/2025' could not be parsed: Invalid date 'APRIL 31'
Text '15/08/2025' could not be parsed: Unable to obtain LocalDate from
    TemporalAccessor: {MonthOfYear=8, YearOfEra=2025, DayOfMonth=15},ISO of type
    java.time.format.Parsed
blocks.title: Output (the last message is one line; field order may vary; wrapped here)

blocks.text: With the default `SMART` style, `31/04/2025` is silently clamped to 30 April, which is rarely what validating user input wants. Use `ResolverStyle.STRICT` for input validation. The last line is a second trap: with `STRICT`, the pattern letter `yyyy` (year-of-era) cannot produce a date without an era, so parsing fails with a confusing message; with `STRICT`, write `uuuu`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Parsing a date-time with a formatter that lacks the needed fields fails at the end, not at the start: `LocalDate.parse("2025-01-01T10:00")` throws because the text contains a time, and `LocalDateTime.parse("2025-01-01")` throws because it has none. Pick the type that matches the text, or use `parseBest`.

### Time zones and DST traps

A `ZoneId` such as `America/New_York` carries the zone's complete history of rules from the IANA time-zone database that ships inside the JDK. Daylight-saving transitions create two awkward situations: a **gap** (clocks jump forward, some local times do not exist) and an **overlap** (clocks jump back, some local times happen twice). `java.time` resolves both deterministically, as the program below shows for New York in 2024.

blocks.title: Dst.java

blocks.code:
$ java Dst.java
plusDays(1)  : 2024-03-10T12:00-04:00[America/New_York]
plusHours(24): 2024-03-10T13:00-04:00[America/New_York]
hours between: 23
gap  : 2024-03-10T03:30-04:00[America/New_York]
overlap first : 2024-11-03T01:30-04:00[America/New_York]
overlap second: 2024-11-03T01:30-05:00[America/New_York]
day length: PT25H
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
Reading the output:

- On 10 March 2024 at 02:00 New York clocks jumped to 03:00. `plusDays(1)` keeps the wall-clock time (12:00 the next day) and `plusHours(24)` adds exactly 24 hours (13:00 on the wall clock). Between the two results there are only 23 real hours. Choose by intent: "same time tomorrow" is `plusDays`; "24 hours from now" is `plusHours` or `Duration`.
- 02:30 on that day does not exist. `ZonedDateTime.of` moves it forward by the length of the gap to 03:30.
- On 3 November 01:30 occurs twice. By default you get the earlier offset (-04:00); `withLaterOffsetAtOverlap()` selects the later one (-05:00). That day lasts 25 hours.

#### Rules that keep you out of trouble

1. Store and transmit moments as `Instant` (or UTC `OffsetDateTime`); convert to a zone only for display.
2. For future events in a user's local time (a meeting at 09:00 in Berlin next March), store the `LocalDateTime` plus the `ZoneId`, not the UTC instant, because zone rules can change before the event.
3. Never use `LocalDateTime` for a moment that must be unambiguous (log timestamps, payments, tokens). It has no zone, so it is not a point on the timeline.
4. Set the JVM or process zone deliberately (`-Duser.timezone=UTC` or `TZ`) and prefer to pass explicit `ZoneId`s.
5. Use `ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata")`, not `"IST"` and not fixed offsets, when you need DST or historical rules.
6. Do not compute age or durations by dividing milliseconds by 86,400,000. Use `Period`, `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between` or `Duration` on the right types.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Which `java.time` class would you use to store the creation time of an order, and why? `Instant`, stored in UTC (a `timestamp with time zone` or `timestamptz` column, or an `OffsetDateTime` at UTC). It is an unambiguous point on the timeline and is independent of server and user time zones. Convert to `ZonedDateTime` for display in the user's zone. `LocalDateTime` is wrong because the same value means different moments in different zones.

### Clock: testing code that uses the current time

Calling `LocalDate.now()` or `Instant.now()` directly inside business logic makes that logic impossible to test deterministically ("is the token expired?" depends on when the test runs). Every `now()` has an overload that accepts a `java.time.Clock`. Inject the `Clock` into your service: production uses `Clock.systemUTC()`, tests use `Clock.fixed(...)` or a small mutable clock.

blocks.title: Svc.java

$ java Svc.java
Token[value=abc, expires=2025-01-01T10:30:00Z]
valid now: true
valid after 29 min: true
valid after 31 min: false
blocks.title: Output

blocks.text:
The test needed no `Thread.sleep` and runs in microseconds. In a Spring application declare a `Clock` bean and inject it; the same trick works for `Random` and UUID generators. For measuring elapsed time inside one JVM use `System.nanoTime()` (monotonic, unaffected by clock adjustments), not `Instant.now()` differences, which can jump when the OS clock is corrected.

### Mapping to databases, JSON and legacy code

- **JDBC 4.2 and later** can read and write `java.time` directly: `rs.getObject("created", OffsetDateTime.class)` and `ps.setObject(1, instant.atOffset(ZoneOffset.UTC))`. Map `DATE` to `LocalDate`, `TIME` to `LocalTime`, `TIMESTAMP` to `LocalDateTime` and `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` to `OffsetDateTime`. Support for `Instant` directly varies by driver; going through `OffsetDateTime` at UTC is portable. The old `java.sql.Timestamp` converts with `Timestamp.from(instant)` and `toInstant()`.
- **JPA/Hibernate 5.2+** maps `java.time` types natively. Avoid the old `@Temporal` annotation, which is for `Date` and `Calendar`.
- **JSON with Jackson**: register `JavaTimeModule` (Spring Boot does) and disable `WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS` to get ISO 8601 strings like `2025-01-01T10:00:00Z` instead of numeric arrays. ISO strings are self-describing and sortable.
- **REST APIs**: send ISO 8601 with an offset or `Z` for moments, plain `2025-08-15` for dates. Avoid pre-formatted local strings like `15/08/2025`.
- **Legacy code**: convert at the boundary and keep `java.time` inside. `Date.toInstant()`, `Date.from(Instant)`, `Calendar.toInstant()`, `Timestamp.toLocalDateTime()`.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: The classic production incident: a service stores `LocalDateTime.now()` in a database on a server in UTC, and a reporting job running in a different zone interprets the same values as local time, so every report is off by the zone offset, twice a year by an extra hour. Using `Instant` or UTC `OffsetDateTime` end to end removes the entire category of bug.

### A worked example: billing dates and calendar arithmetic

Calendar rules appear everywhere in business code: subscriptions that renew monthly, due dates that move off weekends, birthdays on 29 February. The program below puts the earlier types to work and exposes two classic traps.

blocks.title: Bill.java

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- A monthly schedule starting on the 31st must be computed as `start.plusMonths(i)` from the *original* date. The result for February is the 28th (clamped), then March is back on the 31st. Adding one month repeatedly (`d =` `d.plusMonths(1)`) drifts: after 28 February the next addition gives 28 March, not 31 March, and the error never recovers (`2025-04-28` instead of `2025-04-30`).
- `nextBusinessDay` skips weekends using the `DayOfWeek` enum. Real systems add a holiday calendar (a `Set<LocalDate>`) to the same loop. Do not hard-code "add two days if Saturday" rules; loop until the date is valid.
- `YearMonth` models "a month of a year" (credit-card expiry, monthly reports) and knows its length and last day. `Year`, `MonthDay` (for birthdays and anniversaries) and `DayOfWeek` complete the family.
- `TemporalAdjusters.dayOfWeekInMonth(4, THURSDAY)` returns the fourth Thursday of the month: 27 November 2025, the date of US Thanksgiving.
- `Period.between` handles the leap-day birthday rule: someone born on 29 February 2000 is 24 years old on 28 February 2025 and 25 on 1 March 2025. If your business rule differs (some jurisdictions treat 28 February as the birthday), you must code that rule explicitly.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Write date logic as small pure functions that take a `LocalDate` (or a `Clock`) and return a value, and test them with a table of inputs that includes month ends, 29 February, daylight-saving changeover days and year boundaries. Those are the dates that break production, and they are cheap to test.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Use the type that matches the meaning: `Instant` for moments, `LocalDate` for calendar dates, `ZonedDateTime` for user-facing local times, `Duration` and `Period` for amounts.

- All `java.time` types are immutable and thread-safe; arithmetic returns new objects. Months run 1 to 12 and invalid dates throw.
- Store and transmit UTC instants; convert to a zone only for display, and use region ids such as `Asia/Kolkata`.
- `DateTimeFormatter` is thread-safe; use `ResolverStyle.STRICT` and `uuuu` for validation, and pass a `Locale`.
- DST makes some local times missing or doubled and some days 23 or 25 hours long: `plusDays` and `plusHours` differ.
- Inject a `Clock` instead of calling `now()` in business logic so time-dependent code is testable.
#### Strings in depth

items.question: What does this print? `String s = "a"; s.concat("b"); s.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(s);`
items.answer: It prints `a`. Both calls return new strings that are discarded; `String` never changes in place.

items.question: Given `String x = "hi"; String y = new String("hi");`, what are `x == y`, `x.equals(y)` and `x == y.intern()`?
items.answer: `false`, `true`, `true`. `==` compares references; `intern()` returns the pooled instance, which is the same object as the literal `x`.

items.question: Why is `for (...) s += item;` slow for large inputs, and what do you use instead?
items.answer: Each `+=` allocates a new string and copies all earlier characters, so the total work is quadratic. Use `StringBuilder` (or `String.join`, `Collectors.joining`).

items.question: What does `"a,,b,,".split(",").length` return? How would you keep the trailing empty parts?
items.answer: `3` (parts `a`, empty, `b`; trailing empties are dropped). Use `split(",", -1)` to keep them (gives 5).

items.question: Name two reasons `String` is immutable and one consequence for the string pool.
items.answer: Safe map keys / cached hash, security of names and paths, thread safety. Because content never changes, the JVM can safely share one pooled object among all uses of a literal.

items.question: What is the difference between `trim()` and `strip()`, and between `StringBuilder` and `StringBuffer`?
items.answer: `trim` removes chars up to U+0020 only; `strip` (Java 11) removes all Unicode whitespace. `StringBuffer` is synchronized and legacy; `StringBuilder` is the unsynchronised, faster default.

blocks.text: #### Formatting, regex and text

items.question: What does `System.out.printf("[%6.2f] [%-4s] [%04d]%n", 3.14159, "ab", 7);` print?
items.answer: `[ 3.14] [ab ] [0007]` followed by a line break: width 6 with 2 decimals, left-justified width 4, zero-padded width 4.

items.question: What does `"2026".matches("\\d")` return, and what would `Pattern.compile("\\d").matcher("2026").find()` return?
items.answer: `false` (the whole string must match one digit); `true` (find searches for a single digit anywhere).

items.question: `"<a><b>".replaceAll("<.+>", "X")` versus `"<a><b>".replaceAll("<.+?>", "X")`: what does each return?
items.answer: `X` (greedy matches `<a><b>` as one) and `XX` (lazy matches each tag separately).

items.question: Why is `"1.5".split(".")` a bug, and what is the fix?
items.answer: The argument is a regex where `.` matches any character, so the result is an empty array. Use `split("\\.")` or `split(Pattern.quote("."))`.

items.question: Why should a `Pattern` normally be a `static final` field?
items.answer: Compiling is costly and a `Pattern` is immutable and thread-safe, so one shared instance avoids repeated compilation; `Matcher` instances are created per use.

items.question: What makes this text block end with a newline, and how do you avoid it?
items.answer: The closing `"""` sits on its own line after the last text line. Place it at the end of the last text line, or end that line with `\`, to omit the trailing newline.

blocks.text: #### Unicode, charsets and Locale

items.question: What do `"a\uD83D\uDE00".length()` and `"a\uD83D\uDE00".codePointCount(0, 3)` return?
items.answer: `3` and `2`: three UTF-16 units (a plus the surrogate pair), two code points.

items.question: Why can `"é".equals("é")` be false although both print as é? How do you compare them correctly?
items.answer: The first is one precomposed code point, the second is `e` plus a combining accent (two code points). Normalise both with `Normalizer.normalize(s, Normalizer.Form.NFC)` and then compare.

items.question: You decode the bytes of a UTF-8 file with `new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1)`. What do you get and does Java throw?
items.answer: A string of the wrong content (mojibake such as `cafÃ©`, with one char per byte). No exception: Latin-1 can decode any byte.

items.question: What is wrong with `if (input.toLowerCase().equals("title"))`, and what is the fix?
items.answer: `toLowerCase()` uses the default locale; in Turkish `TITLE` becomes `tıtle` and the test fails. Use `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` or `equalsIgnoreCase`.

items.question: What does `NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.GERMANY).parse("12abc")` return?
items.answer: `12` (as a `Long`); parsing stops at `a` without error. Use a `ParsePosition` to detect unconsumed input.

items.question: Which default charset applies to `new String(bytes)` in Java 21, and which in Java 11 on Windows?
items.answer: UTF-8 in Java 18 and later (JEP 400); in Java 11 the platform charset, usually `windows-1252` on a Western Windows installation.

blocks.text: #### Numbers beyond primitives

items.question: What does this print: `System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")));`? What would you use instead?
items.answer: `false`: `equals` compares scale as well as value. Use `compareTo(...) == 0`.

items.question: Why is `new BigDecimal(0.1)` a bad idea? Give two correct alternatives.
items.answer: It converts the inexact `double` literally and gives 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... Use `new` `BigDecimal("0.1")` or `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)`.

items.question: What happens with `BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal("3"))` and how do you fix it?
items.answer: It throws `ArithmeticException` (non-terminating decimal expansion). Supply a scale and rounding mode, for example `divide(d, 5, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)`, or a `MathContext`.

items.question: What do `Math.round(-2.5)`, `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` and `-7 % 2` return?
items.answer: `-2` (rounds half up towards +infinity), `-2147483648` (overflow, still negative), and `-1` (the remainder takes the sign of the dividend).

items.question: Which random class do you use to generate a password-reset token, and which for dice in a multi-threaded simulation?
items.answer: `SecureRandom` for the token; `ThreadLocalRandom.current()` for the simulation.

items.question: What is the difference between the scale and the precision of `new BigDecimal("12.340")`?
items.answer: Scale is 3 (digits after the point); precision is 5 (significant digits: 1, 2, 3, 4, 0).

blocks.text: #### Date and time with java.time

items.question: What does `LocalDate.of(2025, 1, 31).plusMonths(1)` return?
items.answer: `2025-02-28`: the day-of-month is clamped to the last valid day.

items.question: Why is `new Date(2025, 0, 1)` a bug, and what does a modern replacement look like?
items.answer: The `Date(int, int, int)` constructor counts the year from 1900 and months from 0, so it means 3925-01-01 (it is deprecated). Use `LocalDate.of(2025, 1, 1)`.

items.question: What is the difference between `Duration` and `Period`? Which one can you build from two `LocalDate`s?
items.answer: `Period` is date-based (years, months, days); `Duration` is time-based (seconds and nanos) and needs a time-of-day. `Period.between(LocalDate, LocalDate)` works; `Duration.between` on two `LocalDate`s throws.

items.question: Which pattern letter pair gives the wrong year around 31 December: `yyyy` or `YYYY`?
items.answer: `YYYY` is the week-based year; use `yyyy` (or `uuuu`).

items.question: In `America/New_York`, what is `ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 9, 12, 0, 0, 0, ny).plusDays(1)` compared with `.plusHours(24)`, and why do they differ?
items.answer: `plusDays(1)` keeps the wall-clock time (12:00 on 10 March); `plusHours(24)` adds exactly 24 real hours (13:00) because the clocks sprang forward at 02:00 that day.

items.question: Which type would you put in a JSON API field for "when the invoice was paid", and which for "the customer's birthday"?
items.answer: An ISO 8601 instant (`Instant` or UTC `OffsetDateTime`) for the payment time; a `LocalDate` (`1999-04-12`) for the birthday.
